exampleAnswers.title: Applying the Rule of the Lazy Statistician for Discrete Random Variables

question.text:
A discrete random variable $X$ has the probability mass function $f(x)$ shown in the table below. Find $\textrm{E}\big[(X-1)^2\big].$

$x$ $1$ $2$ $3$
$f(x)$ $0.1$ $0.3$ $0.6$
question.explanation:
For a discrete random variable $X$ and a function $r(x),$ the rule of the lazy statistician states that

\[ \textrm{E}[r(X)] = \sum_{x \in S} r(x) f(x). \]

In our case, we have

\[ r(x)=(x-1)^2. \]

Therefore, we obtain

\begin{align} \textrm{E}\big[ (X-1)^2 \big] &=\sum_{x \in S} (x-1)^2 \, f(x) \\[3pt] &= (1-1)^2 \cdot 0.1 + (2-1)^2 \cdot 0.3 + (3-1)^2\cdot 0.6 \\[5pt] &= 0 \cdot 0.1 + 1\cdot 0.3 + 4\cdot 0.6 \\[5pt] &= 0 +0.3 +2.4 \\[5pt] &= 2.7. \end{align}

question.text:
A discrete random variable $X$ has the probability mass function $f(x)$ shown in the table below. Find $\textrm{E}\left[\dfrac{1}{X^2}\right].$

$x$ $\dfrac{1}{4}$ $\dfrac{1}{3}$ $\dfrac{1}{2}$
$f(x)$ $0.3$ $0.2$ $0.5$
question.explanation:
For a discrete random variable $X$ and a function $r(x),$ the rule of the lazy statistician states that

\[ \textrm{E}[r(X)] = \sum_{x \in S} r(x) f(x). \]

In our case, we have

\[ r(x)=\dfrac{1}{x^2}. \]

Therefore, we obtain

\begin{align} \textrm{E}\left[ \dfrac{1}{X^2} \right] &=\sum_{x \in S} \dfrac{1}{x^2} \, f(x) \\[3pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^2} \cdot 0.3 + \dfrac{1}{\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^2} \cdot 0.2 + \dfrac{1}{\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2}\cdot 0.5 \\[5pt] &= 16 \cdot 0.3 + 9\cdot 0.2 + 4\cdot 0.5 \\[5pt] &= 4.8 +1.8 +2 \\[5pt] &= 8.6. \end{align}

question.text:
A discrete random variable $X$ has the probability mass function $f(x)$ shown in the table below. Find $\textrm{E}\big[\sqrt[3] {X}\big].$

$x$ $8$ $27$ $64$
$f(x)$ $0.4$ $0.4$ $0.2$
question.explanation:
For a discrete random variable $X$ and a function $r(x),$ the rule of the lazy statistician states that

\[ \textrm{E}[r(X)] = \sum_{x \in S} r(x) f(x). \]

In our case, we have

\[ r(x)=\sqrt[3]{x}. \]

Therefore, we obtain

\begin{align} \textrm{E}\big[ \sqrt[3]{X} \big] &=\sum_{x \in S} \sqrt[3]{x} \, f(x) \\[3pt] &= \sqrt[3]{8} \cdot 0.4 + \sqrt[3]{27} \cdot 0.4 + \sqrt[3]{64}\cdot 0.2 \\[5pt] &= 2 \cdot 0.4 + 3 \cdot 0.4 + 4 \cdot 0.2 \\[5pt] &= 0.8 + 1.2 + 0.8 \\[5pt] &= 2.8. \end{align}

question.text:
A discrete random variable $X$ has the probability mass function $f(x)$ shown in the table below. Find $\textrm{E}\big[e^X\big].$

$x$ $-1$ $0$ $1$
$f(x)$ $\dfrac{1}{8}$ $\dfrac{3}{4}$ $\dfrac{1}{8}$
question.explanation:
For a discrete random variable $X$ and a function $r(x),$ the rule of the lazy statistician states that

\[ \textrm{E}[r(X)] = \sum_{x \in S} r(x) f(x). \]

In our case, we have

\[ r(x)=e^x. \]

Therefore, we obtain

\begin{align} \textrm{E}\big[e^X\big] &= \sum_{x\in S}e^x \, f(x)\\[3pt] &= e^{-1} \cdot \dfrac{1}{8} + e^0 \cdot \dfrac{3}{4} + e^1 \cdot \dfrac{1}{8} \\[5pt] &= e^{-1} \cdot \dfrac{1}{8} + 1 \cdot \dfrac{3}{4} + e \cdot \dfrac{1}{8} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{e^{-1}}{8} + \dfrac{3}{4} + \dfrac{e}{8} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{e^{-1} + 6 + e}{8}. \end{align}

question.text:
A discrete random variable $X$ has the probability mass function $f(x)$ shown in the table below. Find $\textrm{E}\big[(2X+1)^2\big].$

$x$ $1$ $2$ $3$
$f(x)$ $0.2$ $0.3$ $0.5$
question.explanation:
For a discrete random variable $X$ and a function $r(x),$ the rule of the lazy statistician states that

\[ \textrm{E}[r(X)] = \sum_{x \in S} r(x) f(x). \]

In our case, we have

\[ r(x)=(2x+1)^2. \]

Therefore, we obtain

\begin{align} \textrm{E}\big[ (2X+1)^2 \big] &=\sum_{x \in S} (2x+1)^2 \, f(x) \\[3pt] &= (2+1)^2 \cdot 0.2 + (4+1)^2 \cdot 0.3 + (6+1)^2\cdot 0.5 \\[5pt] &= 9 \cdot 0.2 + 25\cdot 0.3 + 49\cdot 0.5 \\[5pt] &= 1.8 + 7.5 + 24.5 \\[5pt] &= 33.8. \end{align}

exampleAnswers.title: Applying the Rule of the Lazy Statistician for Continuous Random Variables

question.text: Find $\textrm{E}\big[e^{-3X}\big],$ given that the continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function \[ f(x) = \begin{cases} e^{-x+1},& x\geq 1 \\ 0,&\textrm{otherwise} \end{cases} \]
question.explanation:
For a continuous random variable $X$ and a function $r(x),$ the rule of the lazy statistician states that

\[ \textrm{E}[r(X)] = \int^{\infty}_{-\infty} r(x)f(x) \: \textrm{d}x. \]

In our case, we have

\[ r(x)=e^{-3x}. \]

Therefore, we obtain

\begin{align*} \textrm{E}\big[e^{-3X}\big] &= \int^{\infty}_{-\infty} r(x)f(x) \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{1}^{\infty} e^{-3x} \cdot e^{-x+1} \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{1}^{\infty} e^{-4x+1} \, \textrm dx \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac 14 \big[ e^{-4x+1} \big]_{1}^{\infty} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac 14 (0- e^{-3}) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{4e^3}. \end{align*}

example.title: Applying the Rule of the Lazy Statistician for Continuous Random Variables

question.text: Find $\textrm{E}\big[X^3-2X\big],$ given that the continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function \[ f(x) = \dfrac{x^2}{9}, \qquad 0 \leq x \leq 3. \]
question.explanation:
For a continuous random variable $X$ and a function $r(x),$ the rule of the lazy statistician states that

\[ \textrm{E}[r(X)] = \int^{\infty}_{-\infty} r(x)f(x) \: \textrm{d}x. \]

In our case, we have

\[ r(x)=x^3-2x. \]

Therefore, we obtain

\begin{align*} \textrm E\big[X^3-2X\big] &= \int^{\infty}_{-\infty} r(x)f(x) \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^3 (x^3-2x) \cdot \dfrac{x^2}{9} \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^3 \left(\dfrac{x^5}{9} - \dfrac{2x^3}{9} \right) \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \left[ \dfrac{x^6}{54} - \dfrac{x^4}{18} \right]_{0}^3 \\[5pt] &= \left[ \dfrac{27}{2} - \dfrac{9}{2} \right] - 0 \\[5pt] &= 9. \end{align*}

example.title: Applying the Rule of the Lazy Statistician for Continuous Random Variables

question.text: Find $\textrm{E}\left[\dfrac 1X\right],$ given that the continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function \[ f(x) = \begin{cases} 4xe^{-2x},& x\geq 0 \\ 0,&\textrm{otherwise} \end{cases} \]
question.explanation:
For a continuous random variable $X$ and a function $r(x),$ the rule of the lazy statistician states that

\[ \textrm{E}[r(X)] = \int^{\infty}_{-\infty} r(x)f(x) \: \textrm{d}x. \]

In our case, we have

\[ r(x)=\dfrac 1x. \]

Therefore, we obtain

\begin{align*} \textrm{E}\left[\dfrac 1X\right] &= \int^{\infty}_{-\infty} r(x)f(x) \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{\infty} \dfrac 1x \cdot 4xe^{-2x} \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= 4 \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-2x} \, \textrm dx \\[5pt] &= -2 \big[ e^{-2x} \big]_{0}^{\infty} \\[5pt] &= -2(0- 1) \\[5pt] &= 2. \end{align*}

example.title: Applying the Rule of the Lazy Statistician for Continuous Random Variables

question.text: Find $\textrm{E}\left[\dfrac{13X}{1-X}\right],$ given that the continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function \[ f(x) = \dfrac{12}{13}(1-x)^2, \qquad -\dfrac{1}{2} \leq x \leq \dfrac{1}{2}. \]
question.explanation:
For a continuous random variable $X$ and a function $r(x),$ the rule of the lazy statistician states that

\[ \textrm{E}[r(X)] = \int^{\infty}_{-\infty} r(x)f(x) \: \textrm{d}x. \]

In our case, we have

\[ r(x)=\dfrac{13x}{1-x}. \]

Therefore, we obtain

\begin{align*} \textrm E\left[\dfrac{13X}{1-X}\right] &= \int^{\infty}_{-\infty} r(x)f(x) \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{-1/2}^{1/2} \dfrac{13x}{1-x} \cdot \dfrac{12}{13}(1-x)^2 \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{-1/2}^{1/2} 12x(1-x) \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= 12\int_{-1/2}^{1/2} (x-x^2) \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= 12\left[ \dfrac{1}{2}x^2-\dfrac{1}{3}x^3\right]_{-1/2}^{1/2} \\[5pt] &= 12\left[\left(\dfrac{1}{8}-\dfrac{1}{24}\right)-\left(\dfrac{1}{8}+\dfrac{1}{24}\right)\right] \\[5pt] &= 12\left(-\dfrac{1}{12}\right) \\[5pt] &=-1. \end{align*}

question.text: Find $\textrm{E}\big[X^2\big],$ given that the continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function \[ f(x) = \dfrac{x+2}{8}, \qquad -2 \leq x \leq 2. \]
question.explanation:
For a continuous random variable $X$ and a function $r(x),$ the rule of the lazy statistician states that

\[ \textrm{E}[r(X)] = \int^{\infty}_{-\infty} r(x)f(x) \: \textrm{d}x. \]

In our case, we have

\[ r(x)=x^2. \]

Therefore, we obtain

\begin{align*} \textrm E\big[X^2\big] &= \int^{\infty}_{-\infty} r(x)f(x) \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{-2}^2 x^2 \cdot \dfrac{x+2}{8} \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{-2}^2 \left(\dfrac{x^3}{8} + \dfrac{x^2}{4} \right) \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \left[ \dfrac{x^4}{32} + \dfrac{x^3}{12} \right]_{-2}^2 \\[5pt] &= \left[ \dfrac{16}{32} + \dfrac{8}{12} \right] - \left[ \dfrac{16}{32} - \dfrac{8}{12} \right] \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{16}{12} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{4}{3}. \end{align*}

Expressing the integrand in the following equation as a polynomial, we have
question.explanation:
For a continuous random variable $X$ and a function $r(x)$, the rule of the lazy statistician states that

\[ \textrm{E}[r(x)] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} r(x)f(x) ~ \textrm{d}x, \]

where $f(x)$ is the probability density function of $X.$

In this problem, $X$ is chosen uniformly from $[0,1]$, so the probability density function is

\[ f(x) = 1, \:\:\:\:\:\: 0 \leq x < 1. \]

Let $A$ denote the area of the triangle formed by the three points $(0,0), (2,0),$ and $(2,X).$ The triangle has a fixed base of length $2$ along the $x$-axis, and a height of length $X$ from $(2,0)$ to $(2,X).$ Using the standard formula for the area of a triangle, we have

\begin{align*} A &= \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \textrm{base} \cdot \textrm{height} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot 2 \cdot X \\[5pt] &= X. \end{align*}

So, we define

\[ r(x) = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{x}. \]

We now apply the rule of the lazy statistician:

\begin{align*} \textrm{E}\left[A\right] &= \int^{\infty}_{-\infty} r(x)f(x) \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} x \cdot 1 \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} x \, \textrm dx \\[5pt] &=\left[ \dfrac{x^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{1} \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{1}{2}}. \end{align*}

question.text:
A stick of length $2$ is broken at a point chosen uniformly at random along its length. Let the continuous random variable $X$ denote the distance from the left end of the stick to the break point, and let $Y=Y(X)$ denote the length of the longest piece.

Expressing the integrands in the following equation as polynomials, we have
question.explanation:
For a continuous random variable $X$ and a function $r(x)$, the rule of the lazy statistician states that

\[ \textrm{E}[r(x)] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} r(x)f(x) ~ \textrm{d}x, \]

where $f(x)$ is the probability density function of $X.$

In this problem, the break point $X$ is chosen uniformly from $[0,2]$, so the probability density function is

\[ f(x) = \dfrac{1}{2}, \:\:\:\:\:\: 0 \leq x < 2. \]

When the stick is broken at point $X$, it is divided into two pieces: one of length $X$ and the other of length $2-X.$ The longer of the two pieces, $Y$, is therefore given by

\[ Y = \textrm{max}(X, 2-X). \]

Therefore, we define

\[ r(x) = \textrm{max}(x,2-x). \]

To evaluate the integral, we express $r(x)$ as an explicit piecewise function. Observe that,

  • if $0\leq x\leq 1$, then $x\leq 2-x$, so the longer piece has length $2-x$,

  • if $1 < x \leq 2$, then $x > 2 - x$, so the longer piece has length $x.$

Therefore,

\[ r(x) = \begin{cases} 2-x, & 0 \leq x \leq 1, \\ x, & 1 < x \leq 2. \end{cases} \]

We now apply the rule of the lazy statistician:

\begin{align*} \textrm{E}\left[Y\right] &= \textrm{E}\left[\textrm{max}(X, 2-X)\right] \\[5pt] &= \int^{\infty}_{-\infty} r(x)f(x) \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{(2-x) \cdot \dfrac{1}{2}} \: \textrm{d}x + \int_{1}^{2} \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{x\cdot \dfrac{1}{2}} \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{1} (2-x) \: \textrm{d}x + \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{1}^{2} x \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} \left[2x - \dfrac{x^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{1} + \dfrac{1}{2} \left[\dfrac{x^{2}}{2}\right]_{1}^{2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(2-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) + \dfrac{1}{2}\left(2-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\[5pt] &= 2-\dfrac{1}{2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{2}. \end{align*}

Therefore, the expected length of the longer piece is $\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{3}{2}}.$

question.text:
A stick of length $6$ is broken at a point chosen uniformly at random along its length. Let the continuous random variable $X$ denote the distance from the left end of the stick to the break point, and let $Y=Y(X)$ denote the length of the shortest piece.

Expressing the integrands in the following equation as polynomials, we have
question.explanation:
For a continuous random variable $X$ and a function $r(x)$, the rule of the lazy statistician states that

\[ \textrm{E}[r(x)] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} r(x)f(x) ~ \textrm{d}x, \]

where $f(x)$ is the probability density function of $X.$

In this problem, the break point $X$ is chosen uniformly from $[0,6]$, so the probability density function is

\[ f(x) = \dfrac{1}{6}, \:\:\:\:\:\: 0 \leq x < 6. \]

When the stick is broken at point $X$, it is divided into two pieces: one of length $X$ and the other of length $6-X.$ The shorter of the two pieces, $Y$, is therefore given by

\[ Y = \textrm{min}(X, 6-X). \]

Therefore, we define

\[ r(x) = \textrm{min}(x,6-x). \]

To evaluate the integral, we express $r(x)$ as an explicit piecewise function. Observe that,

  • if $0\leq x < 3$, then $x < 6-x$, so the shorter piece has length $x$,

  • if $3 \leq x \leq 6$, then $x \geq 6 - x$, so the shorter piece has length $6-x.$

Therefore,

\[ r(x) = \begin{cases} x, & 0 \leq x < 3, \\[5pt] 6-x, & 3 \leq x \leq 6. \end{cases} \]

We now apply the rule of the lazy statistician:

\begin{align*} \textrm{E}\left[Y\right] &= \textrm{E}\left[\textrm{min}(X, 6-X)\right] \\[5pt] &= \int^{\infty}_{-\infty} r(x)f(x) \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{3} \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{x \cdot \dfrac{1}{6}} \: \textrm{d}x + \int_{3}^{6} \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{(6-x)\cdot \dfrac{1}{6}} \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{6} \int_{0}^{3} x \: \textrm{d}x + \dfrac{1}{6} \int_{3}^{6} (6-x) \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{6} \left[\dfrac{x^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{3} + \dfrac{1}{6} \left[6x - \dfrac{x^{2}}{2}\right]_{3}^{6} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{6}\left(\dfrac{9}{2}\right) + \dfrac{1}{6}\left[(36-18)-\left(18-\dfrac{9}{2}\right)\right] \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{4} + \dfrac{1}{6}\left(18-\dfrac{27}{2}\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{4} + \dfrac{1}{6}\left(\dfrac{9}{2}\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{4} + \dfrac{3}{4} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{2}. \end{align*}

Therefore, the expected length of the shorter piece is $\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{3}{2}}.$

question.text:
A stick of length $2$ is broken at a point chosen uniformly at random along its length. Let the continuous random variable $X$ denote the distance from the left end of the stick to the break point, and let $Y=Y(X)$ denote the length of the shortest piece.

Expressing the integrands in the following equation as polynomials, we have
question.explanation:
For a continuous random variable $X$ and a function $r(x)$, the rule of the lazy statistician states that

\[ \textrm{E}[r(x)] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} r(x)f(x) ~ \textrm{d}x, \]

where $f(x)$ is the probability density function of $X.$

In this problem, the break point $X$ is chosen uniformly from $[0,2]$, so the probability density function is

\[ f(x) = \dfrac{1}{2}, \:\:\:\:\:\: 0 \leq x < 2. \]

When the stick is broken at point $X$, it is divided into two pieces: one of length $X$ and the other of length $2-X.$ The shorter of the two pieces, $Y$, is therefore given by

\[ Y = \textrm{min}(X, 2-X). \]

Therefore, we define

\[ r(x) = \textrm{min}(x,2-x). \]

To evaluate the integral, we express $r(x)$ as an explicit piecewise function. Observe that,

  • if $0\leq x < 1$, then $x < 2-x$, so the shorter piece has length $x$,

  • if $1 \leq x \leq 2$, then $x \geq 2 - x$, so the shorter piece has length $2-x.$

Therefore,

\[ r(x) = \begin{cases} x, & 0 \leq x < 1, \\ 2-x, & 1 \leq x \leq 2. \end{cases} \]

We now apply the rule of the lazy statistician:

\begin{align*} \textrm{E}\left[Y\right] &= \textrm{E}\left[\textrm{min}(X, 2-X)\right] \\[5pt] &= \int^{\infty}_{-\infty} r(x)f(x) \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{x \cdot \dfrac{1}{2}} \: \textrm{d}x + \int_{1}^{2} \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{(2-x)\cdot \dfrac{1}{2}} \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{1} x \: \textrm{d}x + \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{1}^{2} (2-x) \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} \left[\dfrac{x^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{1} + \dfrac{1}{2} \left[2x - \dfrac{x^{2}}{2}\right]_{1}^{2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) + \dfrac{1}{2}\left[(4-2)-\left(2-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\right] \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{2}\left(2-\dfrac{3}{2}\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{4} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2}. \end{align*}

Therefore, the expected length of the shorter piece is $\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{1}{2}}.$
